questions.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java?
questions.title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Checked exceptions** are verified by the compiler — you must either catch them or declare them with `throws`. **Unchecked exceptions** (RuntimeException subclasses) are not enforced by the compiler. Checked exceptions model recoverable external failures; unchecked exceptions model programming bugs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core Java knowledge — one of the most frequently asked exception questions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not being able to give examples of each type
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the design philosophy: checked = external failures you must handle, unchecked = your bugs

sections.title: Checked vs Unchecked
sections.content:
| Aspect | Checked Exception | Unchecked Exception |
|---|---|---|
| Compiler enforcement | Must handle or declare | Not required |
| Parent class | Exception (not RuntimeException) | RuntimeException |
| Examples | IOException, SQLException, ClassNotFoundException | NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException |
| Typical cause | External resource failure | Programming bug |
| When to use | Caller can meaningfully recover | Bug that should be fixed |

sections.title: The Design Philosophy
sections.content:
The split exists because:

**Checked exceptions** model situations where the caller has a genuine chance to recover. A file not found? Maybe ask the user for a different path. A network timeout? Maybe retry. These are external failures — worth forcing the caller to think about.

**Unchecked exceptions** model programming bugs. If you got a NullPointerException, there's nothing useful to catch — the code is wrong and needs fixing. Forcing callers to catch every NPE would create unreadable code.

This philosophy is why `IOException` is checked but `NullPointerException` is unchecked.

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: So the key difference is compiler enforcement. Checked exceptions — like IOException or SQLException — the compiler forces you to either catch them or declare them with throws on the method signature. Unchecked exceptions — like NullPointerException or IllegalArgumentException — the compiler doesn't check at all. The design rationale is that checked exceptions are for external failures where the caller might meaningfully recover, like a file not found. Unchecked exceptions are for programming bugs — there's no point forcing you to catch a NullPointerException everywhere; the real fix is to not have nulls. In practice, modern frameworks like Spring tend to use unchecked exceptions to avoid cluttering method signatures.

groups.heading: Checked exceptions
groups.text: Checked exceptions extend Exception but not RuntimeException. The compiler verifies you've handled them — you must either catch them or declare throws on the method. They model external failures where recovery is possible: file not found, database down, network timeout.

groups.heading: Unchecked exceptions
groups.text: Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException. The compiler doesn't care if you handle them. They model programming bugs — accessing null, going past array bounds, passing illegal arguments. The fix is to write correct code, not to catch the symptom.

items: Use checked when the caller can genuinely recover — file not found, retry a network call.
Use unchecked when the failure is a bug — fix the null, fix the bad index, fix the wrong argument.
In Spring applications, prefer unchecked to keep method signatures clean; use @ControllerAdvice at the top.

beats.text: non-obvious: Spring converts SQLException (checked) to DataAccessException (unchecked) so your service layer doesn't need a throws clause about JDBC internals. The caller that can handle a DB failure still can — unchecked exceptions are still catchable.

speakable_v2.cap: Checked = compiler forces you to handle external failures; unchecked = bugs you should fix instead of catch.

questions.question: Can you give examples of commonly used checked exceptions in Java?
questions.title: Common Checked Exceptions in Java
questions.direct_answer: Common checked exceptions include **IOException** (file/network I/O), **SQLException** (database operations), **ClassNotFoundException** (reflection/class loading), **InterruptedException** (thread interruption), and **ParseException** (date/number parsing failures).

sections.title: Common Checked Exceptions
sections.content:
- **IOException** — reading/writing files, network streams; parent of FileNotFoundException, SocketException
- **SQLException** — any database operation via JDBC
- **ClassNotFoundException** — used with Class.forName() for dynamic class loading
- **InterruptedException** — thrown when a sleeping or waiting thread is interrupted
- **ParseException** — thrown by SimpleDateFormat.parse() when the date string doesn't match the format
- **FileNotFoundException** — subclass of IOException; specific to missing files

sections.title: Handling Checked Exceptions
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The most common checked exceptions you'll encounter as a Java developer are IOException for file and network operations, SQLException for anything database-related through JDBC, ClassNotFoundException when you use Class.forName() for dynamic loading, InterruptedException when working with threads — that one gets thrown when a sleeping thread is interrupted. Another one is ParseException from SimpleDateFormat when the input string doesn't match the expected date format. All of these represent situations where something outside your code — a file system, network, database — can fail, and Java is forcing you to acknowledge that possibility.

questions.question: Why do modern frameworks like Spring prefer unchecked exceptions?
questions.title: Why Spring Uses Unchecked Exceptions
questions.direct_answer: Spring converts most checked exceptions (like `SQLException`) to **unchecked** equivalents (like `DataAccessException`) because checked exceptions pollute method signatures up the call stack, force callers to handle exceptions they cannot recover from, and make code harder to read without adding safety.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the checked exception controversy and Spring's design choice
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Spring wraps checked exceptions — many freshers don't realize DataAccessException is unchecked
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain exception translation and the concept of 'handle it or it propagates automatically'

sections.title: The Problem with Checked Exceptions at Scale
sections.content:
Checked exceptions have a **propagation problem**. If a DAO method throws `SQLException`, every method in the call chain — service, controller — must either catch it or declare `throws SQLException`. This:

1. **Pollutes signatures** — your service layer now knows about JDBC details
2. **Forces meaningless catches** — most callers can't recover from a database failure anyway
3. **Breaks abstraction** — the database implementation leaks into the API

Spring's solution: **exception translation**. Spring catches `SQLException` in its JDBC/JPA layer and rethrows it as `DataAccessException` — which is an unchecked `RuntimeException`. Callers that can handle it do; others let it propagate naturally.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy wraps all JDBC/JPA checked exceptions
- This follows the 'exception translation' pattern
- Callers who can recover still can — RuntimeException is catchable
- Method signatures stay clean — no throws clauses propagating through layers
- This is why @Repository beans automatically get exception translation in Spring

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Spring prefers unchecked exceptions because checked exceptions create a propagation problem. Imagine your DAO throws SQLException — now your service layer, your controller, every layer up the chain has to either catch it or declare throws SQLException. That's messy and breaks abstraction because now your web layer knows your app uses JDBC. Spring solves this with exception translation: it catches the checked SQLException and rethrows it as an unchecked DataAccessException. Callers who can meaningfully handle a database failure still can — unchecked exceptions are still catchable. But callers who can't just let it propagate up to a global exception handler. The result is cleaner code with no throws clauses polluting every method signature.

beats.text: Spring converts checked exceptions to unchecked ones through a pattern called exception translation. The classic example: JDBC's SQLException is checked, but Spring's DataAccessException is unchecked. Spring catches one and rethrows the other so your business code stays clean.

questions.question: What happens at compile time if you don't handle a checked exception?
questions.title: Compile Error for Unhandled Checked Exception
questions.direct_answer: The Java compiler throws a **compile-time error**: 'unreported exception X; must be caught or declared to be thrown'. You must either wrap the code in a try-catch or add `throws ExceptionType` to the method signature.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of how the compiler enforces checked exception handling
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing 'not handled at compile time' with 'won't fail at runtime' — unchecked still fails at runtime
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain both options: catch it locally, or declare it and push responsibility to the caller

sections.title: Compile Error Example
Key Points
sections.content:
- The compiler error is: 'unreported exception X; must be caught or declared to be thrown'
- Option 1: catch it — handle the exception in the current method
- Option 2: declare with throws — pass the responsibility to the caller
- Declaring with throws doesn't handle the exception, it just shifts the obligation
- If main() declares throws Exception, the JVM handles uncaught exceptions

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: If you don't handle a checked exception, you get a compile-time error saying 'unreported exception, must be caught or declared to be thrown'. The compiler gives you two options: either wrap the code in a try-catch to handle it right there, or add throws to your method signature to push the responsibility to whoever calls your method. The key insight is that declaring throws doesn't solve the problem — it just moves it one level up. Eventually someone in the call chain has to catch it. Many freshers add throws to every method just to make the compiler happy, which is actually bad practice because it defeats the purpose of checked exceptions.

This is Java's design contract for checked exceptions: someone in the call chain must acknowledge and decide what to do with this failure. The compiler makes sure that acknowledgment happens somewhere.

speakable_v2.cap: You must catch or declare every checked exception; always choose the option that reflects who can actually handle the failure.

questions.question: How do you wrap a checked exception in an unchecked exception?
questions.title: Wrapping Checked Exception as Unchecked in Java
questions.direct_answer: You catch the checked exception and re-throw it wrapped in a **RuntimeException** (or a custom unchecked exception). Pass the original as the **cause** to preserve the full stack trace. This is the **exception translation** pattern used extensively by frameworks like Spring.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical exception handling — how to translate exceptions across layers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrapping without passing the original as cause — losing the original stack trace
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Create a custom unchecked exception class and explain when wrapping is appropriate

sections.title: Wrapping a Checked Exception
Key Points
sections.content:
- Always pass the original exception as the cause: new RuntimeException(message, cause)
- Without the cause, you lose the original stack trace — very hard to debug
- Create a custom unchecked exception rather than throwing RuntimeException directly
- This is the foundation of Spring's exception translation mechanism
- The caller can still catch your custom exception if needed

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The pattern is to catch the checked exception and rethrow it wrapped in a RuntimeException or a custom unchecked exception. The critical thing is to always pass the original exception as the cause — so you do new RuntimeException(message, originalException). If you don't pass the cause, you lose the original stack trace and debugging in production becomes a nightmare. In practice, you'd create a custom unchecked exception class for your layer — like DataAccessException — rather than throwing plain RuntimeException. This way callers who want to handle the specific failure still can, but callers who can't just let it propagate.

beats.text: Wrapping a checked exception means catching it and rethrowing it as an unchecked RuntimeException subclass. This converts the checked nature to unchecked so the exception can propagate freely without forcing every caller to declare throws.

You wrap when you're crossing a layer boundary and don't want the lower layer's exception type to leak up. A service layer shouldn't throw SQLException — that reveals the JDBC implementation. Instead it throws DataException, which is its own vocabulary.

Throwing plain RuntimeException instead of a named exception — callers can't catch it specifically.
Wrapping every layer — only wrap at boundary crossings, not in every method.

questions.question: Why is InterruptedException a checked exception?
questions.title: Why InterruptedException is Checked
questions.direct_answer: **InterruptedException** is checked because thread interruption is an external, intentional signal — another thread explicitly called `interrupt()` on yours. The compiler forces you to acknowledge this signal so you don't accidentally swallow it, which would break cooperative thread cancellation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of thread interruption as a design mechanism, not just an exception
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Swallowing InterruptedException with an empty catch block — breaks the interruption contract
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the correct handling: re-interrupt the thread after catching

sections.title: Why InterruptedException is Checked
sections.content:
Thread interruption in Java is a **cooperative mechanism**. When `Thread.sleep()` or `Object.wait()` is interrupted, it throws `InterruptedException`. The compiler makes it checked because:

1. Another thread explicitly sent you a signal — you must decide what to do
2. If you silently swallow it (empty catch), the thread continues as if nothing happened — breaking cancellation logic

The correct handling options:
- **Re-interrupt** the thread: `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` — restores the interrupted status
- **Propagate** it: declare `throws InterruptedException`
- **Convert** to RuntimeException (wrapping) — least preferred

sections.title: Correct Handling of InterruptedException
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: InterruptedException is checked because thread interruption is a deliberate cooperative signal — some other thread explicitly called interrupt() on yours. The compiler forces you to handle it because if you silently swallow it with an empty catch, you've broken the interruption contract. The thread that interrupted you probably wanted to cancel your task, and now it's still running. The correct way to handle it is either to re-interrupt the current thread by calling Thread.currentThread().interrupt() after catching, which restores the interrupted flag, or to propagate it up with throws InterruptedException. What you should never do is catch it and ignore it.

seo.metaTitle: Why InterruptedException is Checked | Java Interview Questions for Freshers

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 REST service throwing custom exceptions for invalid input
familiarity_anchors: swallowing InterruptedException with an empty catch block
speakable_v2.hook: Swallowing InterruptedException isn't just bad practice — it silently breaks your app's ability to shut down cleanly.

beats.text: InterruptedException is checked because thread interruption is an intentional cooperative signal, not a bug. When another thread calls interrupt() on yours, Java clears the interrupted flag and throws InterruptedException from sleep() or wait(). The compiler forces you to acknowledge it.

Thread interruption is how Java implements cooperative cancellation. An executor shutting down sends interrupt signals to its threads. If a thread silently swallows InterruptedException, it ignores the cancellation request and keeps running — that's why the compiler forces you to handle it.

items: Option 1: re-interrupt the thread — Thread.currentThread().interrupt() — restores the interrupted flag so callers can check it
Option 2: propagate — declare throws InterruptedException and let the caller decide
Option 3 (last resort): wrap as RuntimeException — only if you truly can't propagate

beats.text: production trap: An empty catch block on InterruptedException is common in fresher code. In production, when the application server tries to shut down, executor threads ignore the interrupt signal and block graceful shutdown — the server hangs for 30 seconds waiting for threads that refuse to stop.

items: Empty catch block on InterruptedException — silently breaks cooperative cancellation in thread pools.
Forgetting to re-interrupt after catching — the interrupted flag is cleared when the exception is thrown.
Wrapping as RuntimeException without re-interrupting — higher callers can't detect the interrupt.

speakable_v2.cap: InterruptedException is checked because ignoring it silently breaks cooperative thread cancellation — always re-interrupt or propagate.
